strengths: Clear problem formulation: Well-motivated extension of SAM3 to handle complex natural language instructions beyond short noun phrases
Sensible technical approach: Hierarchical instruction taxonomy (concept→simple→complex) with cascaded adapters reflects linguistic complexity progression naturally
Thorough data pipeline: Three-stage annotation-inspection-correction workflow ensures high-quality instruction-mask pairs with diverse semantic types
Comprehensive ablations: Table 2 convincingly demonstrates contribution of curriculum learning, distribution alignment, and hard-region supervision
Parameter efficiency: 1.1B parameters vs 8.8B for agent-based alternatives, with single-pass inference
Clear presentation: Well-written with intuitive figures and logical flow
weaknesses: Explicitly marked as 'preliminary results' with comprehensive evaluation ongoing; unsuitable submission for a fully-realized contribution
Limited evaluation scope: Only evaluated on authors' own PACO-LVIS-Instruct dataset; no validation on established benchmarks (ReferIt, G-Ref, ReasonSeg)
Questionable ACL relevance: Core contribution is image segmentation (computer vision), not NLP; language understanding component is straightforward attribute/spatial reasoning
Incremental technical novelty: Cascaded adapters, curriculum learning, and alignment losses are established techniques; main contribution is combination, not fundamental innovation
Moderate performance gains: 54.0 vs 41.6 on simple (12.4 gIoU improvement) but only 51.0 vs 48.2 on complex (2.8 gIoU); authors explicitly state state-of-the-art is out of scope
Dataset concerns: PACO-LVIS-Instruct constructed using MLLMs (Qwen3-VL) introducing systematic biases; no inter-annotator agreement metrics; acknowledged N-to-1 limitation prevents group reasoning
Limited instruction complexity: Despite 'complex' label, instructions remain relatively simple; no multi-step reasoning or handling of 1-to-N group segmentation
No external validation: No zero-shot generalization studies, cross-dataset evaluation, or comparison with other instruction-following segmentation methods
Incomplete analysis: No systematic error analysis, failure case discussion, or investigation of which linguistic phenomena cause difficulties
Significant computational barriers: Data construction requires 32 H100 GPUs, model training 16 H100s, limiting reproducibility; depends on Qwen3-VL availability

strengths: Clear problem motivation: effectively articulates SAM3's limitation in requiring external agents for complex instructions
Thoughtful data construction pipeline: three-stage annotation-inspection-correction process shows engineering rigor
Intuitive hierarchical instruction taxonomy: concept/simple/complex structure provides clear training progression
Ablation studies demonstrate contributions of major components (curriculum learning, alignment losses, uncertainty supervision)
Open-source commitment with practical fine-tuning workflows supports reproducibility
Clear presentation with effective figures communicating the approach
weaknesses: Fundamental venue mismatch: This is a computer vision paper (segmentation architecture, visual grounding) inappropriately submitted to ACL. The linguistic component is shallow (prompt encoding) rather than substantive CL/NLP contribution.
Preliminary results status: Authors explicitly state 'Preliminary results. Comprehensive evaluation is ongoing' (page 6), indicating incomplete work unsuitable for conference publication

Single-dataset evaluation with no standard benchmarks: Only evaluated on authors' own PACO-LVIS-Instruct. Missing evaluation on ReasonSeg, LISA, and other established instruction-following segmentation benchmarks

Incomplete baseline comparisons: No comparison with other instruction-following segmentation methods; SAM3+Agent comparison is unfair (different system components). Missing recent visual grounding baselines.
No statistical rigor: Lacks significance testing, confidence intervals, error bars, or inter-annotator agreement metrics. No error analysis or failure case investigation.

Data quality and reproducibility concerns: MLLM-heavy annotation/inspection pipeline provides no acceptance rates, rejection statistics, or bias mitigation. Human correction stage lacks documentation of protocols, annotator qualifications, or agreement metrics.

Limited technical novelty: Cascaded adapter insertion into SAM3's text encoder is straightforward. No ablation comparing single vs. dual-adapter designs. Alignment losses are standard techniques. Primary contribution is engineering rather than methodological innovation.

Architectural design lacks justification: Why separate simple/complex branches over unified design? How are conflicting branch predictions reconciled? No sensitivity analysis of loss weighting (Lseg, Lalign, Lhard).

Acknowledged limitations unresolved: N-to-1 instance bias, single-concept limitation, object-only evaluation, no real task evaluation—these are presented as future work, indicating incomplete evaluation
Modest empirical improvements: Complex instruction gIoU of 51.0 shows only marginal gain over agent-based 48.2. Insufficient to justify architectural complexity.
Parameter efficiency overstated: 37.5% parameter increase (0.8B to 1.1B) marketed as 'lightweight'. No timing comparisons for fair computational assessment.
Generalization red flags: Only trained on PACO-LVIS-derived data. No cross-dataset evaluation, zero-shot generalization studies, or out-of-distribution testing.
Dataset construction details sketchy: No information on typical rejection rates, convergence patterns, or why 100% inspection accuracy is achievable. Potential data cherry-picking.
Missing implementation details: Multi-stage training hyperparameters, computational costs, sensitivity to design choices, and reproducibility concerns limit verification.

Weak related work coverage: Referring expression comprehension, visual question answering, and visual grounding connections underdeveloped. Recent instruction-following segmentation work (ReasonSeg, LISA) relegated to future work.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation clearly articulating SAM3's NP-only limitation and the need for complex instruction understanding in real-world applications

Principled hierarchical design: instruction taxonomy (concept→simple→complex) mirrors linguistic complexity; cascaded adapters elegantly preserve backward compatibility while enabling new capabilities

Rigorous data construction pipeline with three-stage process (automatic annotation via MLLM → agentic verification with 100% accuracy requirement → human correction) yielding 843,504 high-quality instruction-mask pairs

Strong experimental validation within scope: maintains SAM3's concept-level performance (48.9/54.1 gIoU/P@50) while achieving substantial gains on simple (54.0/59.6) and complex (51.0/56.4) instructions; comprehensive ablations validate each component
Single-pass inference architecture is computationally advantageous compared to multi-round agent pipelines (1.1B vs. 8.8B parameters)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (data scaling, N-to-1 bias, architectural constraints, limited evaluation scope) demonstrates research maturity
Clear presentation and detailed implementation information support reproducibility; promised open-source release
weaknesses: Critical concern: authors explicitly state results are 'preliminary' with 'comprehensive evaluation ongoing' (footnote p.6), undermining Findings-level soundness claims and suggesting work is insufficiently mature for acceptance

Severely limited evaluation scope: single-dataset evaluation (PACO-LVIS-Instruct only) with no validation on standard referring expression benchmarks (RefCOCO/+ /g, COCO-Ref) or cross-dataset generalization studies

No error analysis, failure case documentation, or breakdown of performance by instruction type; substantial performance gap between simple (54.0) and complex (51.0) instructions unexplained, suggesting undiagnosed instruction understanding failures

Inadequate comparison with related work: no comparison with existing referring expression segmentation models (LISA, ReasonSeg); SAM3+Agent baseline is somewhat weak; missing broader instruction-following vision model comparisons

Insufficient justification for architectural choices: cascaded adapters not compared to LoRA/prefix-tuning alternatives; KL divergence for alignment not justified against other divergences; claim that cascading mirrors linguistic complexity lacks empirical support

Data quality concerns: heavy MLLM dependence (Qwen3-VL) introduces systematic bias; no inter-annotator agreement metrics for human correction; no analysis of instruction quality statistics or diversity

Limited NLP contribution relative to ACL scope: uses existing text encoder and MLLM without proposing novel NLP methods; doesn't address paraphrasing, coreference, pragmatics, or core language understanding phenomena; better suited for vision venue (ICCV/CVPR)

Acknowledged model limitation: primarily trained on N-to-1 instance segmentation, fails on group reasoning (1-to-N), limiting real-world applicability; frozen SAM3 backbone may constrain instruction understanding
Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis on loss function types, hyperparameters, training stage ordering, or adapter design alternatives

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitations of existing instruction-guided segmentation methods that handle only simple NP prompts; hierarchical instruction formulation (concept/simple/complex) is intuitive and well-justified

Substantial dataset contribution: HMPL-Instruct is comprehensive with 44,109 images, 849,792 instructions, 213,160 part-level masks, systematic coverage of instruction hierarchies and granularities, and human-in-the-loop construction with multiple validation stages

Rigorous experimental validation: Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, evaluation on both benchmarks and custom dataset, multi-faceted qualitative analysis with clear insights

Technically sound approach: Cascaded adapter design with clear motivation, multiple specialized losses targeting different aspects, well-designed multi-stage training curriculum, results preserve SAM3's concept capability while adding instruction following
Clear presentation and comprehensive appendices: Well-structured paper with informative figures, detailed implementation details, visualization results, and data construction pipeline documentation
weaknesses: Computational complexity inadequately addressed: No runtime or memory footprint comparisons; multi-stage training with cascaded adapters likely expensive; MLLM-based instruction generation/validation pipeline cost is not analyzed; scalability implications of human-in-the-loop validation not discussed

Limited baseline diversity: Primary comparisons only against SAM3 and SAM3 Agent (same family); missing comparisons with other recent instruction-guided segmentation methods; SAM3 Agent baseline unfairly compared as it wasn't designed for this task

Generalization concerns: All experiments on natural images from PACO-LVIS/COCO; no cross-domain evaluation to medical imaging, satellite imagery, or other visual domains; unclear how hierarchical instruction formulation generalizes beyond this domain

Design choices insufficiently justified: Three-level instruction hierarchy not empirically validated as optimal; weighting scheme in contrastive loss (Eq. 3) lacks theoretical justification; parent-rank anchoring assumes instruction hierarchies that may not always hold; loss weight balance appears empirically tuned

Dataset bias and representativeness: MLLM-based generation may introduce systematic biases; human-in-the-loop filtering with 100% accuracy requirement may bias toward unambiguous instances; limited discussion of whether instruction distribution represents real-world usage

Incomplete analysis of limitations: Brief Limitations section lacking failure mode analysis; no evaluation of ambiguous instructions, negations, or complex logical operators; missing robustness analysis to instruction paraphrasing; no human evaluation of instruction-following quality beyond mask metrics

Limited technical novelty: Cascaded adapters are standard transfer learning approach; loss functions are adaptations of existing techniques; primary novelty is problem formulation and dataset rather than novel architectures or algorithms

Evaluation limitations: gIoU and PaSe don't directly measure instruction-following quality; no inter-annotator agreement reported; missing sensitivity analysis for instruction complexity or ambiguity distribution

Methodological concerns: Freezing SAM3 backbone may unnecessarily limit task-specific learning; multi-stage training strategy lacks clear convergence criteria or stage transition ablation; reproducibility difficult due to MLLM randomness in annotation pipeline
Moderate performance improvements: Concept-level improvement (29.5→30.8 gIoU) is incremental; overall improvements consistent but not dramatic, limiting impact claims

strengths: Clear motivation: The paper identifies a genuine limitation of SAM3 (short NP prompts only) and proposes a reasonable solution for richer natural-language instructions.

Substantial dataset contribution: HMPL-Instruct with ~850K hierarchically-annotated instructions and multi-granularity target labels represents significant effort and could be valuable to the community.
Careful curation methodology: The three-stage construction pipeline (automatic annotation, agentic inspection, human correction) demonstrates methodological rigor in dataset assembly.

Thorough ablation studies: Table 5 systematically validates the contribution of individual components (instruction contrastive loss, parent-rank anchoring loss, mask alignment loss, uncertainty supervision), providing clear evidence of what drives improvements.

Comprehensive experimental scope: Coverage of multiple metrics (gIoU, PaSe), benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefZOM, HMPL-Instruct), and target granularities (one-to-one, one-to-many, one-to-all) provides reasonable breadth.
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: The cascaded adapter mechanism (bottleneck + down-projection/GELU/up-projection) is standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning, not a novel architectural contribution. The four alignment losses are reasonable but straightforward combinations of existing designs (contrastive, ranking, KL divergence losses), not novel techniques.

Misleading framing of 'instruction-following': The system fundamentally relies on external MLLM agents to convert long instructions to short NPs (Fig 2b), contradicting claims of instruction-following. The pipeline includes multiple rounds of mask filtering. The model doesn't follow instructions end-to-end; it delegates interpretation to external agents, undermining the central claim.

Significant dataset construction biases: Instructions are written post-hoc after seeing target objects, introducing annotation bias where annotators naturally align instructions with visible properties rather than organic task formulations. The 'one-to-many' setting is artificially constructed by manual grouping of visually similar instances rather than emerging naturally. Data is bootstrapped from PACO-LVIS, covering only specific object categories.

Modest empirical improvements and lacking statistical rigor: Simple instructions show negligible gIoU improvement (59.7 for both SAM3-I and Agent). Complex instructions show only marginal gains (49.0/51.0 gIoU/PaSe). Table 3 shows SAM3 Agent achieving competitive or superior performance in multiple settings. No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing provided despite small margins.

Unfair experimental comparisons and limited baselines: SAM3-I keeps SAM3 backbone frozen while gaining adapters; SAM3 Agent uses external MLLM—unclear whether improvements derive from architecture or additional capacity. Only compares with SAM3 variants despite citing other instruction-following segmentation methods (Xu et al., 2025; Jang et al., 2025) in related work.

Problematic dataset generalization: All experiments on PACO-LVIS derivatives. Generalization to novel object categories, visual domains, and out-of-distribution instructions is unexplored. The paper acknowledges 'scaling training data for richer instruction knowledge' as a limitation but provides no experiments addressing this.

Heavy reliance on external agents as systemic dependency: Both dataset construction and baseline methods depend on Owen3-VL-8B, creating a single point of failure. If the MLLM changes, the dataset and baselines become inconsistent. This undermines the claimed independence of the instruction-following approach.

Insufficient reproducibility and clarity: Multi-stage training with varying hyperparameters scattered across Appendix D lacks transparency. MLLM prompts for annotation generation not fully specified. Dense presentation conflates multiple contributions (PIS hierarchy, adapter mechanism, dataset). The distinction between 'instruction-following' and 'agentic' approaches is blurred.

Minimal failure analysis and domain coverage: Limited discussion of failure modes—when and why SAM3-I fails, which instruction patterns are problematic, whether certain visual contexts are challenging. Only cherry-picked qualitative examples provided in Fig. 4. No evaluation on truly held-out instruction domains or novel visual categories.

Questionable computational efficiency claims: 311.9M trainable parameters added (0.3B additional). Inference time, memory costs, and computational overhead compared to baselines underexplored despite claims of efficiency advantages. The multiple rounds of mask filtering add latency.

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical limitation of SAM3's noun-phrase-only prompting capability
Technically sound cascaded adapter mechanism with clear hierarchical design enabling progressive instruction complexity
Comprehensive and well-designed loss functions (contrastive, ranking, alignment, hard-region supervision) addressing specific grounding challenges
Strong experimental results with convincing improvements over baselines and thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of each component
Substantial HMPL-Instruct dataset contribution (44,109 images, 849,792 instructions) with rigorous 4-stage construction pipeline and hierarchical semantic organization
Excellent reproducibility support through detailed appendices, comprehensive implementation details, and promised code/dataset release
Clear presentation with informative figures and thorough documentation making the work accessible and reproducible
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—cascaded adapters use standard architecture, losses combine well-known techniques, and multi-stage training is straightforward curriculum learning
Insufficient computational cost analysis—inference latency, memory requirements, and training time not reported; SAM3 Agent comparison lacks efficiency metrics
Dataset cardinality bias inadequately addressed—unclear distribution of instruction-to-instance cardinalities in HMPL-Instruct and what fraction supports truly one-to-many grounding

Complex instructions relatively simple in practice—examples show moderate reasoning tasks rather than genuinely difficult semantic understanding; limited exploration of temporal or multi-step reasoning
Weak baseline comparison using Owen3-VL-8B (not SOTA MLLM) and inherently inefficient multi-step agent approach; no comparison with stronger agents or hybrid methods
Insufficient error analysis lacking systematic categorization of failure modes, performance variation across instruction types, or identification of challenging reasoning patterns
Generalization concerns—all experiments on COCO-based datasets with no out-of-domain evaluation or assessment of transfer across visual domains and instruction styles
Data construction quality concerns—automatic MLLM annotation in Stage 1 lacks bias analysis, inter-annotator agreement metrics missing, annotation quality measures vague
Limited relevance to ACL—core contribution is computer vision (segmentation/grounding) rather than NLP; better aligned with CVPR/ICCV despite instruction-following framing
Minor clarity issues with some notation, unexplained hyperparameter choices, and design decisions lacking sufficient justification
